sources.title: Queen's Pawn Game search result summary (D05 / 2.Nf3 Nf6 branches; snippet only)

overview: This is a crossroads reached by symmetrical knight development: 1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Nf6. Nothing is committed in the centre; the character is decided by White's third move. 3.c4 transposes to Queen's Gambit structures (QGD, Slav, Semi-Slav, QGA) and is by far the most played continuation in the database; 3.g3 gives the Pseudo-Catalan (a Catalan-style fianchetto); 3.e3 with Bd3 and c3 is the Colle; 3.Bf4 or 2.Bf4 is the London; 3.c3 is a flexible quiet set-up. Wikipedia and ChessBase describe the non-c4 lines as closed-centre system play with simple development plans and little theory. Black is generally free to develop logically (...e6, ...c5 or ...c6, ...Bf5/Bg4).

white_ideas.idea: Play 3.c4 to transpose into the Queen's Gambit family and fight for a space advantage.
Colle System: e3, Bd3, c3 and Nbd2, preparing the e3-e4 advance; the dark-squared bishop stays inside the pawn chain until e4 is achieved.
London System: Bf4 outside the pawn chain, e3, c3, Nbd2, Bd3, a pattern played almost independently of what Black does; simple kingside attacking plans.
Pseudo-Catalan with g3 and Bg2: pressure on the queenside and long diagonal (the Catalan idea without c4).

black_ideas.idea: Develop logically with ...e6 and complete development; Black faces no serious danger against Colle or London set-ups.
Challenge the centre with ...c5 for active piece play.
Queenside counterplay with ...b6 and ...Bb7, or ...c6 with ...Bf5/...Bg4 development of the light-squared bishop.
Against g3: mirror with ...g6/...Bg7 and ...O-O, or ...c6 with ...Bg4 (both visible in the most played children).

typical_structures.structure: Closed or tense centre with d4 vs d5 pawns kept on (Queen's Gambit, Catalan, Colle, London).
Colle / London pyramid: White pawns on c3, d4, e3 with a bishop on d3.
Catalan-type fianchetto set-up against a d5/e6 or d5/c6 centre.

character.notes: Quiet at the root. ChessBase says the Colle gives Black comfortable defence with straightforward moves and the London needs minimal theory; Wikipedia describes Queen's Pawn systems leading to closed pawn structures. Catalan is neither extremely sharp nor passive. 3.c4 branches are as sharp as the Queen's Gambit family gets (Semi-Slav) but are not the typical character of this root (own understanding: transposition is common in the data).

gambit.notes: No gambit at the root; 3.c4 is the Queen's Gambit, which is not a true gambit (the pawn is regained).

soundness.notes: Sound for both sides. Catalan used by Kramnik, Anand, Carlsen in title matches; London used by Carlsen and Karjakin (ChessBase). Nothing suggests either side is in difficulty.

structure.notes: Typically closed or tense: centre pawns stay on d4/d5, pieces manoeuvre before contact (Colle, London, Catalan). Wikipedia: Queen's Pawn lines lead to closed pawn structures in the centre. Via 3.c4 the structure may become QGA or Slav-type, which are more open, but those lines belong to their own openings.

approach.notes: The root is a flexible waiting move rather than a system itself, but the lines it leads to for White (London, Colle, Pseudo-Catalan) are systems playable against almost any Black set-up. ChessBase: London is set up almost independently of Black's reaction. Used by elite players (Carlsen, Karjakin for London).

level.notes: For White the Colle and London are low-theory with clear plans, described as having minimal theoretical requirements and simple attacking plans. Catalan/Pseudo-Catalan needs more positional understanding (moderately challenging per Wikipedia). 3.c4 requires learning the Queen's Gambit family. The root itself has little to memorise; the level depends on which third move.

sublines_that_differ.name: Queen's Gambit transpositions
sublines_that_differ.how: Becomes QGD/Slav/Semi-Slav/QGA territory; the most played continuation, with theory-heavy and in places sharp lines.

sublines_that_differ.name: Pseudo-Catalan
sublines_that_differ.how: Fianchetto system; positional, queenside pressure on the long diagonal.

sublines_that_differ.name: Colle System
sublines_that_differ.how: Quiet system aimed at e3-e4; low theory.

sublines_that_differ.name: London System
sublines_that_differ.how: System with the bishop outside the pawn chain; low theory.

sublines_that_differ.name: 3.c3
sublines_that_differ.how: Flexible quiet move, can lead to Colle or London structures.

description.claim: The Symmetrical Variation is a flexible, solid opening that often serves as a gateway to other systems.
description.note: Wikipedia: 2.Nf3 tends to transpose into other lines including the Colle or London.

description.claim: Both sides maintain central influence and prepare to castle without committing to a specific pawn structure.
description.note: True of the root; White's third move decides the structure.

description.claim: It is perfect for strategic players who enjoy outmanoeuvring the opponent in a complex middlegame rather than tactical fireworks.
description.note: Colle and London are described as simple low-theory systems with simple attacking plans; 'complex middlegame' is not what sources emphasise. Taste claim.

common_plans.claim: White: Play c4 to transpose into a Queen's Gambit or Catalan, fighting for a space advantage.
common_plans.note: 3.c4 is the most played continuation; Catalan arises with c4 and g3 together (3.g3 also gives the Pseudo-Catalan without c4).

common_plans.claim: White: Adopt a system set-up like the Colle (e3, c3) or London (Bf4) for solid, low-theory development.
common_plans.note: Colle uses e3 and c3 with Bd3.

common_plans.claim: Black: Challenge the centre with an early ...c5 aiming for active piece play and equality.
common_plans.note: ...c5 is the standard Black response against Colle-type set-ups.

common_plans.claim: Black: Create a solid structure with ...e6 to complete development and neutralise White's central pressure.
